title: Rules Wire a Brain, Not Lists

scenes.tts: An adult human brain has about 86 billion neurons. The genome that builds it has about 20,000 genes that code for proteins. Each neuron connects to many others, so the brain carries on the order of 100 trillion synapses. The genes are fewer than the neurons by a factor of millions. They are fewer than the synapses by a factor of billions. How does the smaller number wire the larger one?
scenes.visual: Three bars grow on a powers-of-ten axis: genes, neurons, synapses. A red question links the short gene bar to the long synapse bar.
scenes.narration: An adult human brain has about 86 billion neurons. The genome that builds it has about 20,000 genes that code for proteins. Each neuron connects to many others, so the brain carries on the order of 100 trillion synapses. The genes are fewer than the neurons by a factor of millions. They are fewer than the synapses by a factor of billions. How does the smaller number wire the larger one?

scenes.tts: Labels are cheap. Take seventy-two genes, and let each one be either on or off in a cell. Every extra gene doubles the number of combinations. Seventy-two genes give about four point seven times ten to the twenty-first labels. That is more than ten billion times the number of neurons.
scenes.caption: Labels are cheap. Take 72 genes, and let each one be either on or off in a cell. Every extra gene doubles the number of combinations. 72 genes give about 4.7 × 10²¹ labels. That is more than ten billion times the number of neurons.
scenes.visual: A row of on/off gene switches; each added switch doubles a count of coloured cell codes 2, 4, 8; then a counter reads 72 genes, 4.7 x 10^21 labels, against the neuron number.
scenes.narration: Labels are cheap. Take 72 genes, and let each one be either on or off in a cell. Every extra gene doubles the number of combinations. 72 genes give about 4.7 × 10²¹ labels. That is more than ten billion times the number of neurons.

scenes.tts: But a label is not a wire. A tag says which cell a neuron is. It says nothing about which of the other 86 billion cells it should connect to. A list with one instruction for each synapse would be billions of times longer than the list of genes. So the information has to be compressed into rules that apply in many places at once.
scenes.visual: One tagged neuron with a ring of cells around it, each marked with a red question mark; a short gene list beside a huge instruction list; the long list folds into a single short rule.
scenes.narration: But a label is not a wire. A tag says which cell a neuron is. It says nothing about which of the other 86 billion cells it should connect to. A list with one instruction for each synapse would be billions of times longer than the list of genes. So the information has to be compressed into rules that apply in many places at once.

scenes.tts: The first rule is a gradient, a molecule whose amount rises smoothly across a tissue. Picture a receptor that is high at one edge of the retina and low at the other. The target holds a matching gradient of a cue that the receptor reads. Each growth cone, the tip of an axon, stops where the signal it senses reaches a set level. One receptor gene and one cue gene place thousands of axons in order.
scenes.visual: Retina on the left with a receptor gradient, target on the right with a cue gradient. Axons grow across; each growth cone halts at its own level, landing in the same order as in the retina.
scenes.narration: The first rule is a gradient, a molecule whose amount rises smoothly across a tissue. Picture a receptor that is high at one edge of the retina and low at the other. The target holds a matching gradient of a cue that the receptor reads. Each growth cone, the tip of an axon, stops where the signal it senses reaches a set level. One receptor gene and one cue gene place thousands of axons in order.

scenes.tts: The second rule is to overproduce, then select. Let each axon branch over a wider area than it needs. Neighbouring retinal cells tend to fire together. So keep the branches whose activity matches that of their neighbours, and remove the rest. The tissue measures this after the connections form, so the genome never has to store it.
scenes.visual: Two neighbouring axons spread wide branches over the target and overlap. Neighbours flash together; branches matching their neighbours stay green, others turn red and vanish, leaving tight clusters.
scenes.narration: The second rule is to overproduce, then select. Let each axon branch over a wider area than it needs. Neighbouring retinal cells tend to fire together. So keep the branches whose activity matches that of their neighbours, and remove the rest. The tissue measures this after the connections form, so the genome never has to store it.

scenes.tts: Now block activity in the eye. Experiments of this kind have often found that the coarse order survives. The fine precision does not. So gradients place the axons roughly, and activity sharpens them. The genome stores rules, and the tissue measures the rest.
scenes.visual: Two panels: with activity, tight clustered terminals in the right order; activity blocked, same order but terminals spread wide.
